checkpoints.prompt: For a workload with 10% usage on weekdays and 90% at month-end, what is the first decision to make to reduce waste with pay-as-you-go pricing?

choices.text: Measure actual usage at month-end and review capacity during normal periods
choices.explanation: With pay-as-you-go pricing, check usage and capacity data separately, and scale up only for the periods when needed.

choices.text: Keep capacity fixed at the month-end peak for the entire period
choices.explanation: This keeps peak capacity even during periods of low usage, so capacity is not adjusted to match usage.

choices.text: Change to the largest instance without measuring usage
choices.explanation: Upsizing without measurement makes it impossible to distinguish the cause of the cost from the performance actually needed.

choices.text: Keep all resources running at all times, even when unused, to avoid pay-as-you-go pricing
choices.explanation: Keeping resources running at all times gives up the cloud benefit of adjusting resources to match usage.

checkpoints.title: Provision resources when needed and review how much you need

checkpoints.prompt: A vulnerable dependency library has been found in an application running on EC2. Which responsibility should the person in charge check first?

choices.text: Create a remediation plan as part of the customer’s responsibility for OS and application updates
choices.explanation: Even when AWS protects the underlying infrastructure, the customer is responsible for the OS and application configuration on EC2.

choices.text: Wait for AWS to automatically update the application dependency library
choices.explanation: The shared responsibility model does not transfer responsibility for maintaining the customer’s applications to AWS.

choices.text: Since responsibility is shared, do not assign anyone to handle updates
choices.explanation: Sharing responsibility does not mean leaving ownership unclear.

choices.text: Ask the person responsible for the physical data center to apply the patch directly
choices.explanation: Protecting physical facilities and managing dependency libraries on EC2 are different layers.

checkpoints.title: What to leave to AWS and what to protect yourself

checkpoints.prompt: Two instances in the same AZ are expected to fail at the same time. Which design is appropriate for separating the failure domain?

choices.text: Place redundant instances in a different AZ
choices.explanation: Using different AZs separates the instances from failure domains shared by a single AZ.

choices.text: Add more instances in the same AZ
choices.explanation: Increasing the number of instances in the same AZ does not change their shared failure domain.

choices.text: Increase the CPU capacity of the same instance
choices.explanation: Changing capacity does not provide isolation from an AZ failure.

choices.text: Change only the Region name to a different name
choices.explanation: Changing the name does not change the actual AZ placement or failure domain.

checkpoints.title: Separate failure domains with Regions and AZs

checkpoints.prompt: For a workload that experiences high demand for just 1 hour each month, the availability requirement is to withstand a 1-AZ failure under normal conditions. Choose 2 correct starting points for comparison.

choices.text: Compare options that increase the required capacity only during periods of high demand.
choices.explanation: Reflecting demand fluctuations over time in capacity planning can help reduce unnecessary costs during normal periods.

choices.text: Compare the cost and benefit of redundancy in a separate AZ to withstand a 1-AZ failure.
choices.explanation: Evaluate the cost alongside the effectiveness of fault isolation in meeting the availability requirement.

choices.text: Always choose the cheapest single-AZ option, ignoring the availability requirement.
choices.explanation: Ignoring the requirement to focus only on cost may fail to meet the necessary availability.

choices.text: Keep maximum capacity fixed regardless of when demand is high.
choices.explanation: Keeping capacity fixed at the peak does not evaluate the trade-off between demand and cost.

checkpoints.title: Design for reasons you can't afford downtime, within the budget available.

checkpoints.prompt: Which option meets the requirement to run a file conversion every night in response to an event, without logging in to the OS?

choices.text: Run Lambda when an event occurs
choices.explanation: Lambda is suited to event-driven processing and does not require users to manage the servers in its execution environment.

choices.text: Manually log in to an always-on EC2 instance and run it
choices.explanation: Always-on operation and manual management do not meet the requirement for event-driven execution with less OS management.

choices.text: Choose S3 as the execution environment
choices.explanation: S3 is an object storage service, not an execution environment for conversion processing.

choices.text: Store the conversion command in DynamoDB
choices.explanation: DynamoDB is a database for key-value access, not an environment for running commands.

checkpoints.title: Compute: Who manages the execution environment?

checkpoints.prompt: Several processes need to retrieve the same image by name, and it does not need to be attached as an individual OS disk. Which storage location is appropriate?

choices.text: Store it as an S3 object
choices.explanation: S3 is a good fit when objects such as images need to be shared by name.

choices.text: Attach a separate EBS volume to each EC2 instance and manage copies
choices.explanation: Managing copies on individual disks complicates the requirement to store shared objects.

choices.text: Store it only in Lambda's temporary execution environment
choices.explanation: Temporary storage is not a persistent shared location for images.

choices.text: Always split the image and store it in an RDS table
choices.explanation: The requirement to store image objects does not make a relational database necessary.

checkpoints.title: Storage: Objects or attached disks

checkpoints.prompt: Choose one service to compare first. You need to search orders by customer ID and date/time, and require table joins and transactions.

choices.text: Consider RDS and check whether it meets the relational query requirements.
choices.explanation: Relational requirements that include joins and transactions are comparison criteria for RDS.

choices.text: Always choose DynamoDB without considering the search conditions.
choices.explanation: DynamoDB centers on key design; it is not something to choose automatically without checking the requirements.

choices.text: Perform joins using only S3 file names.
choices.explanation: S3 object storage does not provide relational joins.

choices.text: Share EBS directly across multiple AZs as a database.
choices.explanation: EBS is an attached disk and does not provide database query capabilities or this sharing method.

checkpoints.title: Database: Querying and operational scope

checkpoints.prompt: When breaking down the three requirements—image uploads, image processing, and order searches—which two combinations of roles are appropriate?

choices.text: Assign image storage to S3 objects
choices.explanation: Images are stored as objects and can be referenced by name during processing.

choices.text: Compare the query characteristics of order searches as requirements for RDS or DynamoDB
choices.explanation: Use the search criteria and operational responsibilities as inputs when choosing a database.

choices.text: Bring all requirements together in manually managed files on EBS
choices.explanation: This ignores the differences between storage formats and query patterns, so it does not break the requirements down by role.

choices.text: Perform image conversion using only the database’s search features
choices.explanation: Conversion is a compute task; choosing a database alone does not explain the execution environment.

checkpoints.title: Combination: Break down requirements by role

checkpoints.prompt: A user logged in successfully, but only a specific S3 operation returned AccessDenied. Which layer should you check next?

choices.text: Evaluation of the principal, action, and resource for authorization
choices.explanation: When an operation is denied after identity has been verified, the next step is to examine the evaluation of the permission policies.

choices.text: Change the login password repeatedly
choices.explanation: Authentication has succeeded, so changing the password does not explain an authorization denial.

choices.text: Shorten only the DNS TTL
choices.explanation: DNS cache does not change the evaluation of IAM permissions for an operation.

choices.text: Make the S3 object public without restriction
choices.explanation: Using public access settings to work around an authorization problem violates least privilege.

checkpoints.title: Authentication and authorization are different questions

checkpoints.prompt: Choose one recommended design. The batch process needs S3 write permissions for only 3 hours.

choices.text: The batch principal assumes a role and runs with temporary credentials.
choices.explanation: Temporary role credentials limit access by purpose and duration, avoiding the distribution of long-term secret keys.

choices.text: Give every developer an administrator access key with no expiration.
choices.explanation: Credentials that are both permanent and overly privileged conflict with role-based and least-privilege design.

choices.text: Make the S3 bucket public anonymously so credentials are unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Anonymous public access does not restrict permissions and cannot allow only the intended writes.

choices.text: Hard-code credentials in the source code.
choices.explanation: Hard-coding secrets in code increases the risks of exposure and makes revocation harder to manage.

checkpoints.title: Principals and roles: Who temporarily becomes what?

checkpoints.prompt: An operation is denied even though the identity policy contains an Allow. Select the two things to check first during evaluation.

choices.text: Check whether there is an explicit Deny for the same principal/action/resource.
choices.explanation: An explicit deny takes precedence over an Allow, so the Allow alone is not enough to determine the outcome.

choices.text: Evaluate the effective permissions, including resource policies and conditions.
choices.explanation: Effective permissions are determined by the combination of multiple policies and conditions.

choices.text: Ignore Deny whenever there is an Allow.
choices.explanation: Ignoring an explicit Deny is an error in IAM evaluation.

choices.text: Allow all actions to resolve the denial.
choices.explanation: Overly broad Allow permissions undermine least privilege without identifying the cause.

checkpoints.title: Policy: Check for Deny as well as Allow

checkpoints.prompt: Choose two appropriate ways to reduce the permissions required by an image-processing Lambda function.

choices.text: Allow only the required prefixes and actions in the target bucket.
choices.explanation: Limiting resources and actions to what the task requires is the principle of least privilege.

choices.text: Issue temporary credentials to the execution role.
choices.explanation: Short-lived credentials limit the impact of a leak compared with long-term keys.

choices.text: Grant the image-processing function administrative permissions for all AWS services.
choices.explanation: Permissions for all services exceed the requirements of the task.

choices.text: Store the key indefinitely in a Lambda environment variable.
choices.explanation: Storing a long-term secret key forfeits the benefits of temporary credentials.

checkpoints.title: Least Privilege and Temporary Credentials

checkpoints.prompt: HTTPS traffic is encrypted, but the encryption settings for the backup stored in S3 have not been checked. What else should you verify?

choices.text: Check the settings for encryption at rest and the key used for decryption.
choices.explanation: TLS protects data in transit, so protection at rest must be checked separately.

choices.text: Assume that HTTPS means no at-rest settings are needed.
choices.explanation: Protection in transit does not guarantee protection for stored data.

choices.text: Remove encryption and recheck only the communication.
choices.explanation: This only weakens protection without addressing the risk at rest.

choices.text: Give everyone permission to decrypt without checking who uses the key.
choices.explanation: Decryption permissions should be limited to the principals that need them.

checkpoints.title: In transit and at rest: Different stages require different protections

checkpoints.prompt: The app can’t read an encrypted object. Select two things to check when troubleshooting KMS.

choices.text: Whether the app’s role has permission to use the key
choices.explanation: Key users need permission to use KMS.

choices.text: Whether the key policy allows that role to use the key
choices.explanation: You need to evaluate the KMS key policy as well as the IAM policy.

choices.text: Changing the key’s name to a shorter one will grant permission
choices.explanation: Renaming the key does not add permission to its policy.

choices.text: Grant kms:* to all principals
choices.explanation: Granting unrestricted permissions does not fix the cause and violates least privilege.

checkpoints.title: KMS: The key itself and permission to use it

checkpoints.prompt: The backup job succeeded. Choose one appropriate way to confirm that the recovery objectives are met.

choices.text: Actually restore to an isolated destination, then verify the data and the time required.
choices.explanation: Successful backup creation alone does not prove that recovery is possible or that the RTO can be met.

choices.text: Judge recovery to be possible based only on the job showing “Success.”
choices.explanation: Backup creation results and restore tests are separate checks.

choices.text: Delete the production data before trying a restore for the first time.
choices.explanation: There is no need to destroy production data for verification.

choices.text: Increase the number of runs without deciding on a restore destination or verification criteria.
choices.explanation: The number of runs alone cannot assess the recovered data or the time required.

checkpoints.title: Backup and restore: Creating a backup and being able to restore from it are different things.

checkpoints.prompt: In a design that passes a DB password to an application, select 2 choices that reduce the exposure surface.

choices.text: Retrieve the password from a managed secret instead of hard-coding it in the code.
choices.explanation: Separating the value from the source code reduces exposure if the code is leaked.

choices.text: Limit the role that reads the secret to only the applications that need it.
choices.explanation: Restricting who can retrieve it supports least privilege.

choices.text: Output the password to logs for troubleshooting.
choices.explanation: Logs are often accessible to a broader audience, so secret values should not be output.

choices.text: Copy the same secret to every developer's environment.
choices.explanation: This increases the number of copies and people who can view them, widening the exposure surface.

checkpoints.title: Secrets: Separate the value, its display, and who can retrieve it.

checkpoints.prompt: SSH to the same IP address succeeds, but HTTPS is the only connection that fails. What should you check separately first?

choices.text: The port used by HTTPS and whether the service is listening on it
choices.explanation: If you can reach the IP address but only a specific service fails, check the port and the service’s entry point separately.

choices.text: Treat the IP address as the port number
choices.explanation: An IP address identifies the host; a port identifies a service entry point on that host. They have different roles.

choices.text: Assume that successful SSH means HTTPS requests are also processed successfully
choices.explanation: A service working on a different port does not guarantee that HTTPS is working.

choices.text: Expose all ports to hide the cause
choices.explanation: Opening all ports does not help isolate the problem; it reduces security.

source.label: IANA service names and port numbers

checkpoints.title: IP and port: Identifying a host and a service

checkpoints.prompt: Which factors should you compare when you want an application to handle retransmissions for small monitoring notifications and avoid connection-establishment delay?

choices.text: Compare UDP’s lightweight nature with the loss-handling measures the application needs.
choices.explanation: UDP does not guarantee delivery, so decide based on the requirements together with the measures the application uses to compensate.

choices.text: Assume UDP always guarantees ordering and retransmission.
choices.explanation: Ordering and retransmission are not standard UDP guarantees.

choices.text: Assume TCP has no delay and needs no retransmission for any use case.
choices.explanation: TCP also has connection and retransmission costs, so compare it against the use case.

choices.text: Get delivery guarantees from port numbers alone, without choosing a transport protocol.
choices.explanation: A port identifies a service; it does not determine delivery characteristics.

checkpoints.title: TCP and UDP: Connection and Delivery Characteristics

checkpoints.prompt: The TLS handshake succeeded, but HTTP 404 was returned. Choose one correct explanation.

choices.text: Transport channel protection succeeded, but HTTP resource routing failed.
choices.explanation: TLS and HTTP are separate layers; a 404 returned after TLS succeeds is an HTTP response.

choices.text: TLS failed too, because the response was 404.
choices.explanation: A 404 is an HTTP response and does not mean that TLS failed.

choices.text: The certificate’s validity can be determined from the HTTP status alone.
choices.explanation: Certificate validation happens during a TLS stage separate from the HTTP status.

choices.text: Disabling TLS will fix the resource routing.
choices.explanation: Removing encryption does not fix an HTTP path problem.

checkpoints.title: HTTP and TLS: The Meaning of Requests and Channel Protection

checkpoints.prompt: Name resolution succeeds and the TCP connection succeeds, but TLS validation fails. What should you check next?

choices.text: Check the certificate name, expiration date, and trust chain.
choices.explanation: When TLS validation fails after DNS and TCP succeed, check the certificate and TLS requirements.

choices.text: Change the CIDR and fix the HTTP status first.
choices.explanation: The TCP connection has already succeeded, and TLS is failing before the request reaches HTTP.

choices.text: Set only the DNS TTL to 0.
choices.explanation: A certificate validation failure after successful name resolution is not necessarily a TTL issue.

choices.text: Change the HTTP application's route and retry TLS.
choices.explanation: The TLS handshake takes place before the HTTP route.

checkpoints.title: Troubleshooting: Work through the layers from the outside in

checkpoints.prompt: The resolver has no stale cache before querying authoritative DNS. What is the next role in name resolution?

choices.text: Follow delegations from the root and proceed to the authoritative DNS for the target zone
choices.explanation: When there is no cache, the resolver follows delegations in the DNS hierarchy to obtain an answer.

choices.text: Send the path directly to the HTTP server to determine the IP address
choices.explanation: HTTP requests come after name resolution; this is not a DNS role.

choices.text: Generate an A record using a TLS certificate
choices.explanation: Certificate validation and DNS record generation are separate responsibilities.

choices.text: Infer the authoritative zone from the port number
choices.explanation: A port is a service entry point and does not determine DNS delegation.

checkpoints.title: Name resolution: From a name to the next query

checkpoints.prompt: Which record should you compare if you want `api.example.test` to act as an alias for `service.example.test`?

choices.text: CNAME
choices.explanation: A CNAME record maps one DNS name to another canonical name.

choices.text: NS
choices.explanation: NS indicates a zone’s authoritative name servers, so it is not typically used for ordinary aliasing.

choices.text: AAAA
choices.explanation: AAAA specifies an IPv6 address; it does not map one name to another.

choices.text: Represent the alias by setting only a TTL
choices.explanation: TTL specifies the cache duration; it does not define a mapping between names.

checkpoints.title: Records: What do they map?

checkpoints.prompt: The TTL of the DNS record is 300 seconds. Which explanation best accounts for some users still connecting to the old IP shortly after a change?

choices.text: A resolver can use a cached answer while time remains on its TTL.
choices.explanation: Because TTL indicates how long a cache entry can be used, changes take time to propagate.

choices.text: TTL is the processing time of an HTTP server, so it does not affect DNS propagation.
choices.explanation: TTL is the period for which DNS cache entries are retained, not HTTP processing time.

choices.text: Changing the TTL immediately clears all existing cache entries.
choices.explanation: A new TTL setting does not immediately clear cache entries that have already been distributed.

choices.text: If the IP is old, the authoritative DNS server must be returning an incorrect answer.
choices.explanation: An old answer can also result from a resolver cache.

checkpoints.title: TTL: How long cached information continues to be used

checkpoints.prompt: The A record returns the expected IP, and TCP 443 succeeded, but the certificate hostname does not match. Which responsibility failed?

choices.text: TLS certificate validation
choices.explanation: After DNS and TCP succeed, a hostname mismatch is a TLS certificate validation problem.

choices.text: DNS name resolution
choices.explanation: Because the expected IP was returned, name resolution succeeded in this observation.

choices.text: HTTP status routing
choices.explanation: TLS has not completed yet, so this is not the HTTP status routing stage.

choices.text: TTL cache retention
choices.explanation: A hostname mismatch does not itself indicate a cache duration.

checkpoints.title: DNS Is the Entry Point: HTTP and TLS Have Separate Responsibilities

checkpoints.prompt: For a /26 CIDR block (the full range of 64 addresses before AWS reservations), select the correct description.

choices.text: Each range of 64 addresses is contiguous and does not overlap with the others.
choices.explanation: A /26 has 6 host bits out of the 32-bit address, giving a range of 64 addresses. The boundaries are also spaced 64 addresses apart.

choices.text: A /26 has 256 addresses each, so the ranges overlap.
choices.explanation: A /26 contains 64 addresses, not 256.

choices.text: The second is fully contained within the first CIDR block.
choices.explanation: 10.0.0.64 is beyond the end of the first /26 and is not contained within it.

choices.text: The prefix length does not affect the number of hosts.
choices.explanation: The prefix length determines how the address is divided between the network and host portions.

checkpoints.title: CIDR: The Prefix Length Is the Length of the Network Portion

checkpoints.prompt: Choose the one appropriate check for the plan to split VPC `10.0.0.0/24` into `10.0.0.0/25` and `10.0.0.128/25`.

choices.text: Confirm that both subnets are contained within the VPC and do not overlap each other.
choices.explanation: When splitting, first check that the child ranges are contained within the parent range and do not overlap each other.

choices.text: Adopt the subnet if it can be reached via a route, even if it is outside the VPC.
choices.explanation: A subnet’s address range must be contained within the VPC.

choices.text: Create overlapping subnets and use routes to determine priority.
choices.explanation: Overlapping CIDRs should be avoided during design; routes are not a way to resolve them.

choices.text: Judge containment by the subnet name alone, without looking at the prefix.
choices.explanation: Containment and overlap are determined by numerical ranges.

checkpoints.title: Split: Check containment and overlap first

checkpoints.prompt: You plan to use a `/28` in an AWS IPv4 subnet. What do you need to consider when estimating the number of usable addresses?

choices.text: Subtract the 5 addresses reserved by AWS from the total number of addresses in the CIDR block.
choices.explanation: AWS reserves 5 addresses in each IPv4 subnet.

choices.text: Assign all 16 addresses in the CIDR block to EC2.
choices.explanation: This overestimates the usable addresses because it does not exclude the addresses reserved by AWS.

choices.text: All 16 addresses in a `/28` are usable because none are reserved.
choices.explanation: AWS-reserved addresses must be taken into account regardless of the prefix length.

choices.text: Determine the number of reserved addresses from the number of route tables.
choices.explanation: The number of reserved addresses is not determined by the number of route tables.

checkpoints.title: AWS-reserved IPs: Not all addresses are usable

checkpoints.prompt: An instance in the subnet has a public IPv4 address, but the route table has no route to an IGW. Which statement correctly determines public reachability?

choices.text: A public IP alone is not enough; also check for a route to the IGW.
choices.explanation: To identify a public subnet in AWS, a route from the route table to an IGW is required.

choices.text: If an instance has a public IP, it can always reach the internet even without a route.
choices.explanation: The presence of an address alone does not create a route.

choices.text: Changing to a private IP makes an IGW route unnecessary.
choices.explanation: Changing the IP does not provide the required route.

choices.text: Public reachability is determined solely by NACL permissions.
choices.explanation: A NACL is only one part of the permissions; it does not replace the route and gateway requirements.

checkpoints.title: Public/private: determined by the route

checkpoints.prompt: A route table contains `10.0.0.0/8` and `10.1.0.0/16`, and the destination is `10.1.2.3`. Which principle determines the route selected?

choices.text: The more specific `10.1.0.0/16` route takes precedence.
choices.explanation: In the same table, longest-prefix match selects the more specific route for the destination.

choices.text: Always select the route that was registered first.
choices.explanation: The deciding factor is how specifically the prefix matches the destination, not the registration order.

choices.text: Select based only on the target name, without checking the CIDR.
choices.explanation: The target is the next hop; it does not determine which destination matches.

choices.text: Always send traffic to both routes simultaneously.
choices.explanation: Ordinary route selection chooses the most specific match.

checkpoints.title: Routes determine the next hop for each destination.

checkpoints.prompt: Choose two components needed to allow only outbound requests from instances in a private subnet to an external API.

choices.text: Add a route from the private subnet’s route table to a NAT gateway.
choices.explanation: A NAT gateway supports outbound traffic from the private side.

choices.text: Provide a route from the NAT gateway to the internet.
choices.explanation: The NAT gateway needs a route on the public side to reach external destinations.

choices.text: Attach an IGW directly to the private instance.
choices.explanation: An IGW is used through a subnet route and public conditions; it does not directly replace the private-side egress design.

choices.text: Open all inbound ports for the external API.
choices.explanation: Allowing all inbound traffic is not required for outbound requests.

checkpoints.title: An IGW enables public reachability; a NAT gateway supports egress from the private side.

checkpoints.prompt: Which option allows return traffic for communication permitted by a security group (SG) without an explicit rule?

choices.text: a stateful security group
choices.explanation: An SG is stateful and handles return traffic for permitted communication based on connection state.

choices.text: only a stateless network ACL
choices.explanation: A network ACL (NACL) is a stateless filter that evaluates the return direction separately as well.

choices.text: route table
choices.explanation: A route table determines the next target and does not manage stateful permissions.

choices.text: DNS record
choices.explanation: A DNS record maps a name to a value and does not manage packet state.

checkpoints.title: Check subnet and instance permissions after routing traffic

checkpoints.prompt: The private service name resolves to the correct IP, and the destination SG already allows the traffic. Which combination should you check next to troubleshoot?

choices.text: Check the sender's route table and subnet ACL, along with the return path.
choices.explanation: Since the name and destination permissions are confirmed, investigate the outbound path and return path separately.

choices.text: Delete the DNS record and add a different name.
choices.explanation: Because the name resolves to the correct IP, changing the record is not the next troubleshooting step.

choices.text: Allow all traffic in the destination SG and skip checking the route.
choices.explanation: Traffic is already allowed, and opening everything would only reduce security.

choices.text: Always add a NAT gateway for private services, too.
choices.explanation: Adding a NAT gateway without checking the routing requirements for the private connection is inappropriate.

checkpoints.title: Troubleshoot private connections by checking names, routes, and permissions separately

checkpoints.prompt: Which is an appropriate purpose of running the same build and tests for every small commit?

choices.text: Shorten the gap between a change and a failure, making it easier to pinpoint what needs fixing
choices.explanation: Frequent automated checks keep the changes at each integration point small and make it easier to trace the cause.

choices.text: Hide failures until the next release
choices.explanation: CI is a mechanism for detecting failures early.

choices.text: Skip tests to make builds faster
choices.explanation: CI aims to check integration quality early; it is not about skipping checks.

choices.text: Combine commits and run a single manual check
choices.explanation: Checking a large set of changes later makes it harder to identify the cause of a failure.

checkpoints.title: CI: Check Small Commits

checkpoints.prompt: What describes a state in which an artifact can be deployed at any time after approval, without being deployed to production automatically?

choices.text: continuous delivery
choices.explanation: Delivery puts validated changes in a deployable state, while execution of deployment can be separated by an approval gate.

choices.text: continuous deployment only
choices.explanation: Deployment means putting changes into a live environment; it is distinct from automatic deployment without approval.

choices.text: source control commit
choices.explanation: A commit records a change; it is not itself the state of having a deployable artifact.

choices.text: rollback
choices.explanation: Rollback is the act of returning to a previous version; it is not a delivery state.

checkpoints.title: Separating delivery from deployment

checkpoints.prompt: Which method is appropriate for proving that the same artifact was used in both the test and production environments?

choices.text: Record the build artifact’s digest and verify that it matches in both environments.
choices.explanation: A digest provides a basis for identifying the same artifact across environments.

choices.text: Rebuild from the source separately for each environment and give the builds the same name.
choices.explanation: Even with the same name, separate builds may have different contents.

choices.text: Match only the deployment times.
choices.explanation: Deployment times do not show that the artifact contents are identical.

choices.text: Resolve dependencies again in production.
choices.explanation: Regenerating artifacts separately for each environment breaks the principle of promoting the same artifact.

checkpoints.title: Build an artifact once and promote it

checkpoints.prompt: When an integration test fails in a pipeline, choose two decisions that safely stop promotion.

choices.text: Treat the failure as a failed gate and stop subsequent stages.
choices.explanation: A quality gate prevents a failed change from advancing to the next stage.

choices.text: Record the cause of failure and the conditions for rerunning, then retest after making the fix.
choices.explanation: Keeping a record through reproduction, fixing, and retesting provides evidence, not just a stop.

choices.text: Ignore the failed stage and proceed to production.
choices.explanation: Ignoring the gate means test results no longer serve as a condition for promotion.

choices.text: Delete the test results and treat the run as successful.
choices.explanation: Deleting the results destroys quality evidence and only hides the failure.

checkpoints.title: Stop at the gate and promote in stages

checkpoints.prompt: What level of test verifies failures that occur only when the HTTP client, DB, and authentication are connected to real services?

choices.text: integration test
choices.explanation: Issues that verify connections among multiple components or external boundaries are covered by integration testing.

choices.text: a unit test for a single function only
choices.explanation: A unit test for a single function does not verify connections between real services.

choices.text: string linting only
choices.explanation: Linting does not verify runtime service integration.

choices.text: image comparison only
choices.explanation: Image comparison alone cannot determine the cause at the HTTP/DB/authentication boundary.

checkpoints.title: Using the right test granularity

checkpoints.prompt: For regression testing a calculation that derives the tax-inclusive amount from the pre-tax amount, with the tax rate changing based on the effective date and time, select two combinations that improve reproducibility.

choices.text: Fix the effective date and time, a 10% tax rate, an amount of ¥1,000, and an expected value of ¥1,100, then compare.
choices.explanation: Fix the effective date and time, tax rate, amount, and expected value as the same inputs so the test can be rerun under the same conditions.

choices.text: Even when testing different effective dates and times, fix a mapping table pairing each date and time with its applicable tax rate and expected value.
choices.explanation: If time dependence remains, fix the mapping between each input date and time, applicable tax rate, and expected value so the test can be rerun.

choices.text: Generate the expected value from the execution result each time.
choices.explanation: If the actual result is used as the expected value, errors cannot be detected.

choices.text: Do not record the inputs and expected value when a failure occurs.
choices.explanation: Information needed to reproduce the issue will be lost.

checkpoints.title: Reproduce with fixed inputs and expected values

checkpoints.prompt: Choose two appropriate conditions for stopping promotion in a release gate that includes required type checks and required integration tests.

choices.text: At least one required integration test failed.
choices.explanation: A required check failure is grounds for not proceeding to the next environment.

choices.text: A required type check failed, and reproduction logs have been saved.
choices.explanation: Because a required type check failed, stop at the gate and review the cause and reproduction logs.

choices.text: The wording of an optional description is slightly different.
choices.explanation: Unless it is an explicitly required quality condition, this may not be an automatic stop condition.

choices.text: All tests passed, so the artifact digest is not checked.
choices.explanation: Passing tests and verifying the identity of the artifact are separate quality conditions.

checkpoints.title: Stopping failures at the quality gate

checkpoints.prompt: A production bug at an input boundary has been reproduced. Choose the one appropriate sequence for preventing it from recurring.

choices.text: Capture the minimal input from the logs, fix the cause, then add a regression test.
choices.explanation: Following the order of minimal reproduction, fixing the cause, and locking in a regression test prevents the same failure from recurring.

choices.text: Delete the logs to hide the fact that the bug recurred.
choices.explanation: Deleting the evidence does not resolve the cause.

choices.text: Rewrite all the code at once without reproducing the issue.
choices.explanation: Large changes made without knowing the cause reduce verifiability.

choices.text: Report that the fix is complete without adding the same test.
choices.explanation: Without a regression test, a recurrence under the same conditions cannot be detected.

checkpoints.title: Investigate the failure and prevent regressions

checkpoints.prompt: Which deployment strategy sends only a small number of users to the new version first, instead of switching everyone at once?

choices.text: canary deployment
choices.explanation: A canary deployment observes the new version with a portion of the traffic before expanding its reach.

choices.text: Rolling out all users in stages only
choices.explanation: This does not describe limiting the rollout to a small number of users; it refers broadly to staged update strategies.

choices.text: Big bang in a single environment
choices.explanation: A big bang switches everyone at once, so it does not narrow the impact scope first.

choices.text: database backup
choices.explanation: A backup is a recovery method, not a deployment strategy.

checkpoints.title: Control the impact scope with deployment strategies

checkpoints.prompt: The canary error rate abort threshold is 2%, and the observed value is 3%. What should you decide next?

choices.text: Record that the abort threshold was exceeded, stop the rollout, and proceed with investigation or recovery.
choices.explanation: The observed value of 3% exceeds the pre-established abort threshold of 2%, so stop the rollout and control the impact.

choices.text: Increase traffic to 100% and dilute the error rate in the average.
choices.explanation: Increasing traffic while the abort threshold is exceeded expands the scope of impact.

choices.text: Rewrite the baseline using the new version’s values.
choices.explanation: Changing the baseline to hide an anomaly undermines the basis for observation.

choices.text: Continue at the scheduled time without measuring the error rate.
choices.explanation: A staged rollout should be guided by observed values and abort criteria.

checkpoints.title: Observe and apply the abort criteria

checkpoints.prompt: The new code has started writing to the old DB schema, and the data format can no longer be read after reverting to the old version. Which recovery decision should you make first?

choices.text: Check DB compatibility and the data recovery point, not just code rollback.
choices.explanation: Reverting the code does not restore data that has already changed, so decide how to recover based on the DB state as well.

choices.text: Deleting the new artifact will also return the DB to its old format.
choices.explanation: Deleting the artifact does not reverse data transformations.

choices.text: Directly delete the DB without checking whether a backup exists.
choices.explanation: Direct deletion increases data loss and destroys recovery points.

choices.text: Assume the incident is resolved if you stop monitoring.
choices.explanation: Stopping observation is not recovery; it only hides the impact.

checkpoints.title: Choose rollback or roll forward

checkpoints.prompt: For database changes made while old and new application versions are running simultaneously, select two steps that improve safety.

choices.text: First perform an expand step, such as adding a backward-compatible column.
choices.explanation: Performing compatible changes that keep the old version running first preserves reads and writes during a gradual rollout.

choices.text: Restore to an isolated environment, then verify the recovered contents and the time required.
choices.explanation: This lets you confirm that the backup can actually be restored without disrupting production.

choices.text: Deploy only the new code first, then immediately stop the old version.
choices.explanation: Switching over without checking compatibility during simultaneous operation leaves fewer recovery options.

choices.text: Remove schema changes from the history to make rollback easier.
choices.explanation: Deleting history does not restore actual data and also loses traceability.

checkpoints.title: Design database compatibility and recovery

checkpoints.prompt: When a single request passes through multiple services, which signal lets you trace which service added latency?

choices.text: trace
choices.explanation: A trace lets you follow the path of one request and the duration of each span.

choices.text: Aggregated metrics only
choices.explanation: Aggregated values show trends but do not directly show the path of one request across services.

choices.text: A single log line only
choices.explanation: A single log line makes it difficult to follow the causal order of the entire request.

choices.text: The SLO name only
choices.explanation: An SLO is a target, not a signal for observing a request's path.

checkpoints.title: Three signals: numbers, events, and request paths

checkpoints.prompt: Choose 2 metrics that directly show user wait time and the growth of a processing queue, respectively.

choices.text: latency
choices.explanation: Directly captures changes in how long users wait.

choices.text: saturation
choices.explanation: A growing queue may indicate insufficient spare capacity in resources or processing capability.

choices.text: traffic
choices.explanation: Traffic shows request volume, but it does not directly indicate the wait time or the state of a processing queue.

choices.text: errors
choices.explanation: Errors show failed requests, but they do not directly indicate the wait time or the state of a processing queue.

checkpoints.title: Four perspectives: Separating user impact from spare capacity

checkpoints.prompt: When defining an SLO that targets a 99.9% success rate, select the two items that must be explicitly specified. Operational settings such as notification recipients and alert thresholds are defined separately.

choices.text: The operations in scope, the success criteria, and the denominator for the success rate
choices.explanation: The SLO cannot be reproduced without specifying what counts as a success and what is used as the denominator.

choices.text: The target value of 99.9% and the observation window
choices.explanation: An SLO must specify the target value and the period over which it is evaluated.

choices.text: Set only the SLO name and decide the denominator later
choices.explanation: Without a defined denominator, the meaning of the success rate changes.

choices.text: Set only notification recipients and alert thresholds, and decide the operations in scope and success criteria later
choices.explanation: Notification recipients and alert thresholds alone cannot define an SLO. Also specify the operations in scope, success criteria, denominator, target, and observation window.

checkpoints.title: SLI, SLO, and alerts: what to notify about, by when, and in what state

checkpoints.prompt: Latency increased after the deploy. Choose one appropriate way to investigate without assuming causation.

choices.text: Compare the same time window and traffic conditions before and after the deploy, then test the hypothesis using traces and logs.
choices.explanation: Align the comparison conditions and use multiple signals to distinguish the hypothesis from causation.

choices.text: Conclude that the deploy alone caused it without investigating other changes made at the same time.
choices.explanation: A conclusion made without investigating simultaneous changes confuses correlation with causation.

choices.text: Delete the latency metric and report an improvement.
choices.explanation: Removing observability does not improve performance.

choices.text: Change the overall SLO based on a single outlier.
choices.explanation: Before changing a target based on a temporary value, you need to check the conditions and trend.

checkpoints.title: Improvement: Test hypotheses and compare results
